newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean won hits 84-month low, further falls seen.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean won hits 84-month low, further falls seen.

text.p: South Korea's currency slumped to its lowest level against the U.S. dollar in 84 months on Thursday and dealers forecast it would depreciate even further despite repeated rescue attempts by the central bank.

The won plunged to 875.30 on spot trading, its weakest level since March 1990 when South Korea introduced the "market average exchange rate system", which determines the rate largely by domestic supply and demand.

"The won continues to post lows against the dollar because the deteriorating current account deficit has upset the balance between demand and supply," said Lee Jang-yung, a research fellow at the Korea Institute of Finance.

Alarmed by the sharp decline in the local currency, the central bank began to sell dollars in forward trading for the first time ever on Tuesday. Traders said it has sold about $500 million over the past three days.
Huh Ko-kwang, director of the central bank's international department, denied that the dollar sales were aimed at boosting the won.
"Beefing up forward trading is essential for the won's future free convertibility. So we need to keep a supply of dollars moving in forward trading to develop it," he said.
The South Korean won is not yet freely convertible.
Huh said daily forward trading volume averaged only about $10 million to $20 million versus $1.30 billion in spot.
After a series of failed attempts to cool steep rises in the dollar, the central bank intervened in spot trading on Thursday morning when the won fell to 875.00.
Spot won closed at 875.00 after opening at 870.00.
Central bank Governor Lee Kyung-shik said on Thursday the current level of the won was acceptable and the central bank's focus was on currency stability.
"I think the current level is acceptable so I want it (the won) to be stable," he told Reuters Financial Television in Bangkok.
But dealers described recent interventions as "absurd" because the dollar's persistent strength against other currencies including the yen and the mark would continue to fuel its rise.
"It's nonsense to (try to) appreciate the won while the dollar is continuously rising in other markets," said a local bank dealer who asked not to be named.
Dealers said the won would continue to depreciate unless economic fundamentals turned around or the dollar stumbled on global financial markets.
They forecast the won would decline to the 880.00-890.00 level in the first half of this year.

South Korea, which suffered a record trade deficit of $20.38 billion last year, was estimated to have posted its biggest current account deficit of $23 billion in 1996. The trade deficit usually represents about 60 percent of the nation's current account shortfall.
Dealers and economists said the trade gap was expected to narrow gradually but they said gloom over the economy's prospects would take its toll on the won.

Despite the won's depreciation, Korean products have not fully benefitted as the falling yen offset much of the potential gains. Korea and Japan compete against each other in overseas markets with similar products.
Dealers said the yen had tumbled 40 percent against the dollar since last June, while the won fell by 10 percent.
A survey by the Korea Foreign Trade Association showed domestic traders believe Korean products would be competitive, if the won fell to the 890.00-900.00 level.
